To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have identified two members of the Fmr gene family in Xenopus tropicaliss, and we have characterized both proteins in terms of tissue distribution, developmental expression pattern, and protein size.
Fmr1 and Xfmr1 are expressed in Xenopus laevis and Xenopus tropicalis, respectively, and that both Fmr1p and Fxr2p show a similar expression pattern in both species.
the expression of the Fxr genes Fmr1 and FXR1 is differentially regulated in Xenopus tropicali s.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification and characterization of the Fxr1 and Fmr1 genes and their gene products Fxr1p and Fmrp in Xenopus laevis and Xenopus tropicalis, respectively.
the characterization of Fmr1 and the Fxr1 gene in X. tropicalis and the identification of the gene products in adult frogs.
the identification, characterization and expression of the Fxr1 gene in X. tropicalis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
both the Fmr1 and the Fxr1 genes are expressed throughout the entire Xenopus tropicalis embryo, but with a different expression pattern.
both Fmrp as well as Fxr1p have a similar function during embryonic development and in the adult animal, although their expression patterns are different.

the Xenopus Fmr1 and the Fxr1 gene are the orthologues of the human FMR1 gene and FXR1 gene, respectively, whereas the Fxr2 gene of the Xenopus tropicalis genome does not represent the orthologue of the human FXR2 gene.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the expression pattern of both Fmr1p and Fxr2p in Xenopus is more similar to the human situation as compared to the mouse situation.
in Xenopus tropicali both Fmrp- and Fxr1-encoding genes were identified and characterized and their tissue-specific expression patterns were described.
the Fmr1 and the Fxr1 genes are expressed in a differentially regulated fashion during Xenopus development and in adult frog tissues.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Fxr gene is not present in Xenopus tropicalissuggesting a more recent evolutionary event in the vertebrate lineage.
Fxr1p, like its human homolog FXR1p, is expressed in striated muscles.
the frog model can be used to study the cellular function of FMRP and FXR1P, respectively, during development and in adulthood.
